title: The Evolving Landscape of Venture Capital Mindsets | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: Martin Casado lays out four idealized VC mindsets (Financial, Productive, Frontier, Speculative) and warns against the 'grab bag trap' of mixing them ad hoc to justify deals. He argues early infrastructure investing should be productive, since tech creates markets and TAM expansion (Uber, GitHub, Cursor) is chronically underestimated.

insights.claim: Venture capital has shifted from loose partnerships of generalists backing speculative emerging tech to coordinated sector teams in large firms, because tech markets matured and available capital grew many orders of magnitude over recent decades.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Large-fund VC behaves more like analytical finance than frontier bet-taking; expect process-driven, metrics-led decisions.
insights.locator: VC investing isn't what it was

insights.claim: Casado wagers that most of the analysis done by modern VC firms is not about technology at all.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Diligence effort at big funds is skewed to finance and market work rather than tech assessment.
insights.quote: In fact, I’d wager most of that analysis isn’t about technology at all.
insights.locator: VC investing isn't what it was

insights.claim: Traditional finance influence on venture is sensible because early-stage companies today are the size of public companies a few decades ago, so evaluating them by metrics and market shape makes sense.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Financial lenses migrated into early venture as company scale grew.

insights.claim: Financial evaluation of metrics and market shape can contradict early-stage tech investing, since tech waves nearly always precede figuring out business models and tech creates the market and TAM, making market-shape evaluation pointless.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Applying TAM and metrics screens to nascent tech systematically misprices it.
insights.quote: Tech waves nearly always precede figuring out the business models.

insights.claim: Casado proposes four archetypal VC philosophies (Financial, Productive, Frontier, Speculative) as a backdrop for deal and fund-strategy discussions, instead of mixing traditional tech-first and finance views into a muddled process.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Use the taxonomy to identify which assumptions an investor is actually betting on.

insights.claim: Financial investors judge assets by business metrics (churn, margin, growth, pricing power, NDR) and TAM, typically invest from early Series B through growth where tech is not the primary differentiator, and are price-sensitive because they back out value from metrics.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Growth-stage, metrics-led investors will anchor valuation to comps and metrics, not technology narratives.

insights.claim: Casado argues most vertical SaaS is not a hard technical problem, so financial investors are best seen as traditional business investors who understand the tech market.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Vertical SaaS should be valued as a business, not as a technology bet.
insights.quote: In fact I would argue most vertical SaaS is not a hard technical problem.

insights.claim: Productive investors treat tech as a market-creating asset, prioritize tech, team and market fit over business metrics, de-emphasize existing TAM and care more about access and exposure to leading technology companies than about deal price.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Productive capital is price-insensitive for category leaders, supporting premium early valuations.

insights.claim: Frontier investing is founder-centric and resembles a talent agency: back the best founders in wildly new spaces and take market risk, on the logic that you cannot predict the future but can diligence a team.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Pre-product rounds are priced on team quality, not market evidence.
insights.quote: The rationale is you can’t predict the future, but you can diligence a team.

insights.claim: Speculative investors, such as crypto token investors and parts of the secondary market, lack visibility into the underlying asset, invest in the market's perception of the deal, emphasize price, macro and market timing, and move in and out of markets across areas and stages.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Token and secondary-market flows are driven by macro and timing, so they can reverse irrespective of company fundamentals.

insights.claim: The philosophies are idealized and no firm strictly follows them, but across many hundreds of deals Casado finds they capture the justifications investors use, and arguments across them talk past each other because they assume different sources of value creation.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Disagreements in deal rooms are often about the underlying framework, not the facts.
insights.quote: it’s hard to directly refute a finance argument with a product argument

insights.claim: The grab bag trap occurs when investors use the philosophies as piecemeal justifications for or against a deal, even though they conflict, for example overweighting TAM or metrics when investing in emerging tech.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Inconsistent objections signal personal bias rather than disciplined process.

insights.claim: Casado recommends a fund or team keep a core philosophy and apply it consistently across deals, flagging when an investment runs contrary to it, because there is no systematic way to resolve tensions between philosophies.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Funds with a stated and consistently applied philosophy should have more predictable behavior and fewer ad hoc misses.
insights.locator: Unfortunately there is no systematic answer

insights.claim: A common mapping of philosophy to stage is pre-product: frontier, pre-traction: productive, post-repeatability: financial; nearly all first-money-in checks are frontier and growth investing is almost entirely financial.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Expect valuation logic to shift from team to metrics as companies cross repeatability.

insights.claim: From seed to early Series C the mapping is unclear because repeatability and market remain uncertain and many companies took years to break out, so Casado cautions against blanket application of a philosophy by stage.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Mid-stage rounds are where philosophy mismatch is most likely, creating mispricing.

insights.claim: Casado describes himself as strictly a productive investor, arguing speculative and financial lenses fit early-stage infrastructure poorly because they discount value created by tech and assume a zero-sum view where upside is capped by existing market size or business models.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: a16z infra bets will favor technology leaders over cheap price or current-metric screens.

insights.claim: Underappreciating TAM expansion is a cliche, with examples of Uber versus taxis, GitHub versus the repository and Cursor versus the IDE, where the new product expanded far beyond the incumbent market.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Sizing disruptive tech by incumbent market understates upside.
insights.quote: Underappreciating TAM expansion is so common it’s almost become a cliche

insights.claim: Casado finds it paradoxical to seek disruptive tech and then judge it with mature-market indicators such as traditional business metrics, though the market is mature enough to allow diligence on approach, target market and founders' company-building views.
insights.speaker: Martin Casado
insights.so_what: Productive investing still involves techno-strategic diligence, not blind faith.
